Write a note to a friend about what your team delivered over the last year and a bit. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the note only.
final_message:
Hi Sam,

It's been a while, so let me give you the short version of what the team has delivered since the spring of last year. I'm rather proud of it.

First, the big one. We finally retired the old case management system, the one you'll remember us grumbling about over coffee. It had been running for nearly fifteen years, held together by workarounds and a handful of people who knew where the bodies were buried. Its replacement is built on open source components, hosted in the cloud, and released in small increments rather than one enormous drop every eighteen months. Staff were using the first working version within four months of kick-off. Not a slide deck, a working service.

Second, we've changed how we buy things. Long contracts with a single supplier left us with exactly one lever to pull whenever something needed to change. We've broken the work into smaller pieces, brought a good deal of the engineering in-house, and opened the door to a wider range of suppliers. It hasn't been painless. Procurement and legal colleagues had to learn a new way of working alongside us, and we had to learn theirs. But the result is that we can now change direction in weeks, not years.

Third, data. For too long every team kept its own spreadsheets and its own definitions, so the same question could get three different answers. We've set up a shared data platform and agreed common standards for the dozen or so datasets that matter most. Early days, but the first cross-team dashboard went live in January, and it's already settled a few long-running arguments.

Fourth, people. We've grown from nine to twenty-six, and I think the hiring is the thing I'm most pleased about. We recruited developers, designers, analysts and a couple of brilliant service managers who had never worked in government before. Several of our existing staff have retrained, and two have moved into product roles. The mix is what makes the difference.

What have we learned? Siloed approaches don't work. Every time we tried to solve a problem alone, we ended up rebuilding something another team had already built. The best moments came when we shared code, shared research and shared mistakes.

There's plenty still to do, and I'd value your view on where to go next. Come and see it in action. I'll buy the coffee.

All the best,
[name]
